clinical_knowledge.topic: Prosthetic Valve Infective Endocarditis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Prosthetic Valve Infective Endocarditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes prompt inpatient admission for blood cultures and empiric IV antibiotics, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: night sweats, persistent fever, and profound tiredness for 4 weeks after dental work

Key HPI features: 4-week history of daily low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats requiring change of bedclothes, severe lethargy, and unintentional 4kg weight loss. Noticed tender, reddish bumps on her fingers last week. Underwent extensive root canal and dental abscess drainage 6 weeks ago without antibiotic cover. Known to have a mechanical mitral valve replacement placed 8 years ago for rheumatic heart disease.

Objective/Exam findings: Check temperature (38.4°C), inspect skin and hands for peripheral immunovascular phenomena: Osler's nodes (tender nodules on finger pads), Janeway lesions (painless erythematous macules on palms/soles), splinter haemorrhages under nails, and Roth spots on fundoscopy. Cardiac auscultation: listen for new or changing mechanical prosthetic regurgitant murmur. Bloods: x3 sets of peripheral blood cultures taken from different sites spaced by at least 1 hour prior to any antibiotics, FBC, CRP, ESR. Transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE - more sensitive than TTE for prosthetic valves).
Relevant background/PMH: rheumatic heart disease, prosthetic mechanical mitral valve replacement (8 years ago), atrial fibrillation
Current medications: warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5), bisoprolol 5mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Prosthetic Valve Infective Endocarditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Occult malignancy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New heart failure, stroke symptoms, or an embolic event.
management_principles: Obtain x3 sets of blood cultures prior to empiric IV antibiotic initiation
Start broad-spectrum IV empiric coverage for prosthetic valve endocarditis (e.g., vancomycin plus gentamicin and rifampicin per local protocol), pending microbiology guidance and culture results
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the management of infective endocarditis

reference_soap.subjective: 64F with mechanical prosthetic mitral valve presents with 4-week fever, night sweats, weight loss, and peripheral stigmata following invasive dental procedures 6 weeks prior.
reference_soap.objective: Check temperature (38.4°C), inspect skin and hands for peripheral immunovascular phenomena: Osler's nodes (tender nodules on finger pads), Janeway lesions (painless erythematous macules on palms/soles), splinter haemorrhages under nails, and Roth spots on fundoscopy. Cardiac auscultation: listen for new or changing mechanical prosthetic regurgitant murmur. Bloods: x3 sets of peripheral blood cultures taken from different sites spaced by at least 1 hour prior to any antibiotics, FBC, CRP, ESR. Transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE - more sensitive than TTE for prosthetic valves).
reference_soap.assessment: Prosthetic valve infective endocarditis (PVIE) following recent invasive dental treatment; determine the organism with blood cultures rather than presuming an oral streptococcus. DDx: occult malignancy, connective tissue disease/systemic lupus, occult dental/deep neck abscess.
reference_soap.plan: Admit immediately for inpatient management. Obtain x3 sets of blood cultures prior to empiric IV antibiotic initiation whenever this does not compromise urgent care. Start empiric IV treatment for prosthetic valve endocarditis with infectious-disease/microbiology input and according to local protocol, then tailor treatment to culture results. Urgent cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery review. Monitor INR closely and assess for embolic complications (stroke, splenic infarction).

learning_objectives: Apply modified Duke criteria for diagnosing infective endocarditis in patients with prosthetic heart valves
Identify classical peripheral immunovascular stigmata: Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages, Roth spots
Explain the imperative of obtaining multiple independent blood culture sets before initiating empirical bactericidal IV antibiotics
Discuss high-risk dental procedures and guidelines surrounding antibiotic prophylaxis in prosthetic valve patients

teaching.one_liner: Bacteria seeded onto a prosthetic heart valve. Fever plus a prosthetic valve is endocarditis until proven otherwise.
red_flags: New heart failure, stroke symptoms, or an embolic event

must_ask.say: How long have you had the fevers, and do they come at a particular time of day?
When did you have your valve surgery, and which valve was replaced?
Have you had any dental work or procedures in the last few months?
Have you lost weight, or been soaking the sheets at night?
Have you had any sudden weakness, vision loss, or painful spots on your fingers?
I ask everyone this — do you use any injected drugs?

history.answer: I have been running a fever and waking up drenched in night sweats for the past month, and I just feel completely exhausted.
The fever started four weeks ago, and it has come back every single day since then.
It usually goes up in the late afternoon to around 38.5 degrees, and I get intense shivering chills with it.
I tried paracetamol a few times, but it only brought my temperature down for a couple of hours before it spiked again.
No, I haven't had any cough, phlegm, sore throat, or trouble catching my breath.
No, I have no burning or pain when I pass urine, no need to go more frequently, and no flank pain.
I haven't had much appetite, but I have not had any stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
I feel exhausted and a bit washed out, but I have no severe headache, stiff neck, or confusion.
I haven't had joint pain or bug bites, but about a week ago I noticed painful, red bumps on the pads of my fingers.
Every night I wake up soaking wet and have to change my clothes, and I have lost four kilograms over the last four weeks without trying.
No, I have not felt any swollen glands or lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No, I haven't traveled anywhere, I don't hike in the woods or work outdoors, and we don't have pets.
No, my husband is completely healthy and nobody around me has been sick.
No, I have never had chemotherapy and I don't take steroids or any medications that weaken my immune system.
I have a mechanical heart valve that was put in eight years ago, and six weeks ago I had an extensive root canal and abscess drained without antibiotics.
No, I haven't started any new prescription medications or over-the-counter pills lately.
I have never used recreational drugs or needles in my life, and I have been in a faithful marriage with my husband for thirty years.
No, I haven't had any sudden arm or leg weakness, numbness, facial drooping, speech difficulty, vision changes, or blood in my urine.
I was wondering if I might have chronic glandular fever, or perhaps that dental infection in my jaw never really went away.
I am really scared about the weight I've dropped and those tender spots on my fingers.
I was hoping you could give me some strong antibiotics to clear up this infection and get my energy back.
I had rheumatic fever as a child that damaged my heart valve, and I also have an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation.
I had open-heart surgery eight years ago to replace my mitral valve with a mechanical valve, but no other surgeries.
I take warfarin every day to keep my blood thin, and bisoprolol five milligrams once daily for my heart rhythm.
No, I don't have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
No, I have never smoked.
I only have an occasional small glass of wine on special holidays.
I am a retired florist, and I live at home with my husband.
My father had a stroke in his eighties, but no one in my family has had heart valve trouble or early heart disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 38.4°C, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air.
Fundoscopy reveals a pale retinal lesion surrounded by hemorrhage in the left eye; conjunctivae are mildly pale without petechiae.
Oropharynx is clear without mucosal lesions or erythema; well-healed recent dental extraction site in the right lower jaw with no fluctuance.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no crackles or wheezes.
Crisp mechanical click audible with a new grade 3/6 holosystolic regurgitant murmur best heard at the apex radiating to the axilla.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender with no voluntary guarding or rebound tenderness.
Spleen tip is palpably enlarged 1 cm below the left costal margin; liver edge is non-tender and not enlarged.
Tender violaceous nodules on two distal finger pads, non-tender red macules on the palms, and linear splinter hemorrhages beneath the fingernails.
Supple neck with full passive range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
